passage: I'm Dolma, and for the clean-lake week I wrote a slogan on chart paper: 'Our lake, our shame, fix it now.' I was proud of it, short and loud. Then my friend Anirban read it and frowned. "Shame? It sounds like you're blaming the whole colony, including the old aunties who've swept that shore for years." I hadn't meant that at all. I meant urgency. I looked at it again and saw that a short line can lean in several directions at once. I tried three more until I found 'Our lake, our care, start today.' My caption for the photo went with it, and it felt warmer. I'm still learning that fewer words means each one carries more.

qa.a: Dolma's first slogan was 'Our lake, our shame, fix it now.'

qa.q: Why did Anirban frown at the word shame?
qa.a: Anirban felt it sounded like blaming the whole colony, including the older neighbours who had cleaned the shore for years. Dolma had meant urgency, so the same words carried a different message for Anirban.

qa.q: What could Dolma try when writing a slogan next time?
qa.a: Show it to a few different people first and ask how each one reads it, then adjust the words.

qa.q: How might one of the aunties who sweep the shore feel about the first slogan?
qa.a: They might feel accused or overlooked, despite their years of work.

grounding: A teen writes a slogan and learns short forms compress attitude and can be read differently by different audiences.

passage: Note, Friday. The Class Nine skit script by Kashish arrived on my desk with the line, 'Everyone in this town is afraid of the truth.' She had also written a caption for the poster: 'Speak up, or stay silent forever.' The words are strong, and I can see she cares about speaking up. But I asked her to imagine how a shy student, or a parent in the audience, might hear them. She was quiet for a bit, then said she hadn't thought of that and wondered if the line sounded like a scolding. She's going to try 'Some of us are afraid of the truth, and that's human.' I will help with the caption too. Avni, drama teacher.

qa.q: What did the poster caption say?
qa.a: The caption said, 'Speak up, or stay silent forever.'

qa.q: What might Kashish have felt when asked how a shy student would hear the line?
qa.a: She may have felt surprised and a bit self-conscious, since she says she hadn't thought of it and wonders if it sounds like scolding. She clearly cares about the message.

qa.q: What could Kashish do with the caption?
qa.a: Try softer, more inclusive wording and test it on a few readers.

qa.q: How might a shy student in the audience feel about the original line?
qa.a: They may feel accused or pressured, instead of invited.

grounding: A teen's script and caption compress attitude, and different audiences read them differently.
